title: The most useful word
text: No word in English {{1}} a stranger career than OK. It was {{2}} in 1839 by a newspaper writer in Boston as a joke — a deliberately illiterate {{3}} of 'all correct', in the fashion for comic abbreviations of the day. The joke should have {{4}} within months. It survived because American politics got hold of it: supporters of President Martin Van Buren, nicknamed Old Kinderhook, formed OK Clubs, and the word {{5}} into permanent usage on the back of a losing campaign. From there it went {{6}}: telegraph operators adopted it for its brevity, radio carried it around the world, and today it is among the most {{7}} words on the planet, needing no translation from Bangkok to Buenos Aires. Linguists {{8}} its success to its shape: two crisp vowels, easy for almost any language to say, meaning neither yes nor no but everything between. A joke that outlived its punchline, OK is now perhaps the most widely understood utterance in human history.

gaps.explanation: 'enjoys a stranger career' — has one worth remarking on; endow = provide with a gift.
'was coined in 1839' — the fixed verb for creating a new word; moan = complain.
'an illiterate spelling of all correct' — the written form; spill = pour out accidentally.
'should have died within months' — faded away; dye = colour fabric, dock = cut short or moor a ship.
'rode into permanent usage on the back of a campaign' — was carried along by it, keeping the image of the phrase 'on the back of'.
'it went everywhere' — spread to all places; the next sentences describe worldwide spread, ruling out the others.
'among the most recognised words on the planet' — known almost universally; relegate = demote.
'linguists credit its success to its shape' — assign the cause to; debit is the accountant's opposite.
